classificationNotes: Regular-audit C4 criteria applied. High reserved for direct asset theft/loss/freeze via a realistic attack path with no hypotheticals. Medium for availability / protocol-function impact or value leak with stated assumptions. Low for state handling / spec deviations. Centralization (C) for findings whose attack vector requires or materially depends on admin action.

DEDUP-001 considered for High but downgraded to Medium: principal is always recoverable via emergencyWithdraw (users forfeit rewards, not principal); there is no single-actor profit path; the 'frozen rewards' outcome requires an extended sequence of recomputes between accrual and claim. This is availability + value-leak with stated assumptions (infrequent claims, frequent interactions), the textbook Medium shape under C4 rules.

DEDUP-003 routed to Centralization: every listed attack scenario begins with a malicious/compromised owner installing a hostile or buggy dispatcher hook. A legitimate owner installing a well-behaved hook does not produce the loss. Kept as C rather than Medium per top-level CLAUDE.md ('centralization risks QA at best' equivalent; we surface as Centralization line-item rather than outright QA because the code-level fix is concrete).

DEDUP-004 routed to Centralization: the only attack path is owner rotating dispatcherHook while old mintDebt is outstanding; finding itself describes it as a 'live-ops footgun' with no external-attacker path. The recommended fix is a defensive code change (totalStaked==0 gate or auto _syncBudget), so we surface as C line-item rather than QA — but it is not Medium because reward loss is recoverable via owner topUp.
No High findings. C4 explicitly discourages severity overstatement; none of the kept findings meet the 'direct theft / permanent freeze with no owner recovery' bar.

findings.title: rewardBudget reset to full balance on every recompute double-counts already-accrued rewards, over-committing emissions and DoSing late claimers

classification.assetImpact: Accrued-but-unclaimed rewards of late claimers can be frozen until owner top-up. Principal always recoverable via emergencyWithdraw.
attackPath: 1. Alice stakes at t=0; rewardBudget set to balance.
2. Time passes; Alice accrues pending rewards, balance unchanged because no interaction has fired _updatePool or a claim.

3. Bob stakes: _syncBudget runs _updatePool (commits Alice's accrual to accRewardPerShare and decrements rewardBudget), then _recomputeSchedule overwrites rewardBudget back to balance (which still includes Alice's committed rewards). windowEnd extended.
4. Over the next window, accRewardPerShare advances against a budget that was already partially spent on paper.
5. First claimer is paid; later claimers hit _safePay shortfall and revert. Earned rewards frozen until owner tops up or users take emergencyWithdraw (forfeiting rewards).
classification.likelihood: medium - no special privilege required; triggered by natural user activity (stake/unstake/claim/topUp/pullAndRefresh) over time. Requires pending accrual to sit uncommitted-to-balance between recomputes, which is the default state between interactions.
classification.assumptions: Pool sees multiple recompute-triggering interactions between a given staker's accrual and their claim. Reward balance does not grow fast enough via pull() / topUp to absorb the over-commitment.
classification.externalRequirements: None external. All triggers are in-protocol.

findings.justification: Assets not directly at risk (principal safe via emergencyWithdraw) but protocol solvency invariant is broken and claim availability is impacted for late claimers — value leak with stated assumptions, textbook C4 Medium.

findings.title: emergencyWithdraw decrements totalStaked without calling _updatePool, retroactively repricing the pre-withdrawal window at the new smaller denominator

classification.assetImpact: Protocol over-emits rewards: forfeited accrual from an emergency-withdrawing staker is redistributed pro-rata to survivors at a re-priced rate, rather than staying with the protocol. Amplifies DEDUP-001 solvency gap.
attackPath: 1. Alice and Bob both stake at t=0, totalStaked=20.
2. Bob calls emergencyWithdraw at t=100. totalStaked drops to 10; lastRewardTime and accRewardPerShare unchanged (no _updatePool).
3. At t=200 Alice claims. _updatePool computes elapsed=200 * rewardRate and divides by current totalStaked=10, crediting Alice for the full [0,200] period at the post-withdrawal denominator.
4. Alice receives ~200R instead of the fair 150R; Bob's forfeited 50R is redirected to Alice rather than retained by the protocol.
classification.likelihood: medium - requires at least one emergencyWithdraw and no intervening _updatePool between that withdrawal and the next settlement. Normal in pools with sparse activity.
classification.assumptions: A user triggers emergencyWithdraw while pool has other active stakers and _updatePool has not been called in the current block.

findings.justification: Protocol-function impact (over-emission beyond nominal rewardRate) with stated assumptions; value leak to survivors. Not direct theft — the surviving staker did not steal, they received over-credited emissions the protocol should have retained. Matches C4 Medium.

findings.title: rewardRate derived from total minted NFT supply but divided by totalStaked allows a lone staker to capture full T-derived emissions at unbounded effective APY

classification.assetImpact: Reward budget is drained far faster than the advertised targetAPY implies when participation is low. Over-emission relative to APY target; late or non-participating NFT holders see runway exhausted before they can stake.
attackPath: 1. Protocol configures targetAPY at MAX=50% against N=100 minted NFTs.
2. Sophisticated actor mints 1 NFT and stakes it alone while totalStaked is tiny (e.g. 1).
3. rewardRate is computed against the full T (all 100 NFTs' notional value) but accRewardPerShare is divided by totalStaked=1 — lone staker captures 100% of the T-derived reward rate.
4. Effective APY on that 1 NFT = targetAPY * (N / totalStaked), unbounded for small totalStaked. Budget depletes ~N times faster than documented.
classification.likelihood: medium - requires low participation. Realistic at launch and during low-TVL periods; sophisticated actors can deliberately stake early and alone.
classification.assumptions: targetAPY is non-zero and totalStaked is small relative to N. No upper cap on individual APY is documented.

findings.justification: Budget drains faster than advertised APY suggests; protocol function (runway predictability) impacted; profit path exists for early lone stakers but not a direct theft — they staked legitimately. Value leak with stated assumptions (low participation). C4 Medium.

findings.title: _recomputeSchedule reads balanceOf(this) directly, allowing donation griefing to extend runway and amplify DEDUP-001

classification.assetImpact: Runway / schedule predictability impacted. No direct fund loss; donors voluntarily subsidise the pool.
attackPath: 1. Owner intends to run setTargetAPY to adjust rate.
2. Attacker front-runs with a 1-wei phUSD transfer to the staker.
3. Subsequent _recomputeSchedule reads the donor-inflated balance into V, extending windowEnd against the over-committed budget.
4. Interacts with DEDUP-001: budget reset wipes prior-emission correction.
classification.likelihood: low - griefing only; no profit motive on its own.
classification.assumptions: Attacker is willing to burn gas for a minor schedule perturbation; interacts meaningfully with DEDUP-001.

findings.justification: State-handling / spec deviation (internal accounting should not trust raw balance reads). No direct asset loss. C4 Low.

findings.title: setTargetAPY settles prior accrual using current totalStaked, mispricing pre-setter period if an emergencyWithdraw has shrunk totalStaked since lastRewardTime

classification.assetImpact: Child of DEDUP-002: minor amplification of over-emission at the APY-change boundary.
attackPath: 1. Alice and Bob stake at t=0 (totalStaked=20).
2. Bob emergencyWithdraws at t=100 without _updatePool running.
3. Owner calls setTargetAPY at t=150; _updatePool uses elapsed=150 but totalStaked=10, over-crediting Alice for the [0,100] window.
4. Fix is the same as DEDUP-002: call _updatePool inside emergencyWithdraw.
classification.likelihood: low - only manifests when an emergencyWithdraw has occurred and no _updatePool has fired since.
classification.assumptions: Owner changes APY while totalStaked has shrunk since lastRewardTime.

findings.justification: State-handling / spec deviation; subordinate to DEDUP-002. No independent attack path. C4 Low.

findings.title: pendingReward view diverges from what claim() actually pays due to stale mintDebt and uncapped-vs-balance computation

classification.assetImpact: UX / integrator impact only. Front-ends may show a 'claimable' value that claim() cannot fulfil or that differs from the paid amount.
attackPath: 1. DEDUP-001 or a pending hook mintDebt creates divergence between stored state and post-claim state.
2. User queries pendingReward, sees value X.
3. User calls claim: reverts on shortfall OR pays a different amount than X because the view did not simulate pull() + _recomputeSchedule.
classification.likelihood: low - UX/integrator impact, not asset impact.
classification.assumptions: Front-end or integrator consumes pendingReward as authoritative claimable value.

findings.justification: View function correctness issue with documented integrator consumers. Not the 'unused view' pattern (has real consumers per finding), but impact is UX / documentation. C4 Low.

findings.title: dispatcher-hook mintDebt() is trusted input to V and windowEnd — malicious or buggy hook can over-commit emissions

classification.assetImpact: Stakers' accrued rewards can be made unpayable (frozen behind _safePay revert) if the owner installs a hostile or buggy dispatcher hook whose mintDebt() overstates inflow vs. pull() actual.
attackPath: 1. Owner (or compromised owner key) installs a dispatcher hook whose mintDebt() returns a huge number but whose pull() mints little or nothing.
2. Natural user activity triggers _syncBudget + _recomputeSchedule; V = balance + hugeMintDebt inflates rewardBudget and windowEnd.
3. Stakers accrue against the inflated schedule; claims start reverting once balance < pending.
4. Recovery: owner topUp, or users take emergencyWithdraw (forfeiting rewards).
classification.likelihood: low - requires owner action to install a bad hook; legitimate owner with well-behaved hook does not produce this loss.
classification.assumptions: Owner is malicious or deploys an untested / buggy hook.
classification.externalRequirements: Owner key controls setDispatcherHook; no totalStaked==0 gate.

findings.justification: Every attack path routes through the owner installing a hostile or buggy hook. Per C4 Universal Invalid + top-level CLAUDE.md ('centralization risks QA at best'), this is centralization. Surfaced as C rather than QA because the recommended fix is a concrete code change (cap V on pull delta, or validate mintDebt against pull inflow).

findings.title: setDispatcherHook rotation orphans the OLD hook's outstanding mintDebt and leaves rewardBudget stale until corrective action

classification.assetImpact: Reward flow can be bricked between rotation and owner corrective action (topUp or hook with matching debt). Principal remains withdrawable via emergencyWithdraw; users forfeit rewards if they take that path.
attackPath: 1. Owner routinely rotates dispatcherHook while the OLD hook still has outstanding mintDebt.
2. Outstanding mintDebt becomes unreachable because pull() now targets the NEW hook.
3. rewardBudget remains inflated from the prior _recomputeSchedule that included old_hook.mintDebt.
4. Subsequent user interactions advance accRewardPerShare against the stale budget until _safePay starts reverting.
5. Recovery: owner topUp or install a replacement hook with sufficient debt to cover the gap.
classification.likelihood: low - requires owner to rotate hook without first calling pullAndRefresh; operational discipline issue, no external-attacker path.
classification.assumptions: Owner rotates dispatcherHook while old hook has non-trivial outstanding mintDebt.
classification.externalRequirements: Owner key controls setDispatcherHook; on-chain workflow does not enforce pre-rotation drain.

findings.justification: Live-ops footgun requiring owner action; no external-attacker path. Finding itself says 'not profitable for an external attacker but a realistic live-ops footgun'. Sister setters (setDispatcherIndex, setNFTMinter) already apply a totalStaked==0 gate and self-healing _recomputeSchedule; this setter is the outlier. Classified as centralization rather than Medium because recovery is always owner-controlled and principal is never at risk.

findings.title: Owner can zero out emissions mid-stake via setTargetAPY(0) or setDispatcherHook(address(0))
findings.justification: Pure centralization risk; explicitly designed-in (setTargetAPY(0) documented as 'supported pause emissions via APY mode' in the spec). QA report only.

findings.title: setPauser accepts address(0) without validation, silently disabling pause/unpause capability
findings.justification: Admin input-validation / reckless-admin-mistake pattern. QA report only.

findings.title: setStakedId does not call _recomputeSchedule, leaving rewardRate / windowEnd stale until the next interaction
findings.justification: State-hygiene / consistency fix between sister admin setters; no external attack path. QA report only.

findings.title: Admin setter input-validation gaps on setDispatcherHook and setNFTMinter
findings.justification: Admin input-validation pattern; owner misconfiguration only; no external attack path. QA report only.
